name: Krasue
origin: Thai folklore, Thailand; kin in Cambodia and Laos
looks: A woman's head floating by itself, glowing faintly, with heart, stomach and entrails trailing from the neck.
behavior: Hunts at night for blood and raw flesh, and must rejoin its hidden body before dawn. Thorny fences and fire hurt it.
license_note: Folklore; a Thai ethnographer's essays record it but the earliest written date is unverified; own description.
sensitivity_note: unverified, wiki only (two Wikipedia pages read, no non-wiki source read). Sightings and village patrols are still reported in Thailand, so it is a living fear. Keep it a monster only; no mockery of real accusations.
reads_at_16x20: yes: round head plus a dangling tail of organs is a clear silhouette

name: Phi Krahang
looks: A shirtless man in a loincloth who flies the night air on two big rice-winnowing baskets used as wings.
behavior: Lives as an ordinary villager by day and flies at night to prey on people walking alone in remote places.
license_note: Folklore; the Ayutthaya-era law texts do not list it, so the name may be later; age unverified.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Recent sightings and an exorcist hire are reported, so it is a living fear. A 2012 case of blaming a real man shows the harm in accusations.
reads_at_16x20: yes: man with two basket wings is distinctive

name: Phi Pop
origin: Thai and Isan folklore, northeast Thailand
looks: Shapeshifting spirit, often seen as a black dog; the host looks like a normal person by day.
behavior: Eats the intestines of sleeping victims and may jump from host to host.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Pop accusations were reported in May 2026 and still push marginalized, often elderly, women out of villages. Owner may prefer to treat it as red; avoid any witch-hunt framing.
reads_at_16x20: yes: black dog silhouette with red eyes

name: Mae Nak
looks: A young mother-ghost who died in childbirth and can stretch her arms to impossible length.
behavior: Stayed beside her returning husband and terrorized the village until a monk trapped her spirit.
license_note: Folklore with a possible real 19th-century base (disputed); own description.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. A real shrine where devotees pray for easy childbirth and leave offerings today; she is treated as a revered figure, not just a monster.

name: Phi Am
looks: A heavy shadow that sits on a sleeper's chest; no fixed body.
behavior: Causes nightmares and the feeling of paralysis in sleep.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. The name is used by ordinary people and medical officials for sleep paralysis today.
reads_at_16x20: no: no clear body; works only as a dark blob

name: Preta
origin: Buddhist cosmology as held in Thailand and India
looks: Very tall, very thin ghost with a mouth like a needle's eye.
behavior: Wanders hungry, never able to eat enough.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Part of living Buddhist teaching (statues stand at Wat Phai Rong Wua); use the monster form only, never a sacred scene.

name: Nang Tani
looks: A young woman in the shadow of a banana clump, seen on full-moon nights.
behavior: Haunts certain banana trees and shows herself at night.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Treated as a living folk belief; the page does not detail present-day practice.

name: Khwai Thanu
looks: A water buffalo made by sorcery, with a magical origin.
behavior: Used by shamans in black magic to attack and harm victims.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. The page says most people believe in it and shamans use it.

name: Phi Phrai
looks: Either a water spirit like an undine, or the ghost of a woman who died with her unborn child.
behavior: Lives in water and lures people there in some tellings (the page is brief).
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Living folk belief; the page does not detail present-day practice.

name: Phi Ya Nang
looks: An elderly woman spirit tied to a boat.
behavior: Possesses a boat as its guardian.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. A protective boat spirit honored by southern Buddhist fishermen and the Royal Thai Navy today. Not an enemy.

name: Aswang (shapeshifter)
other_names: Aswang | ghoul | weredog | viscera sucker | witch
looks: A normal-looking woman by day who becomes a long-tongued hunter, a dog, a pig or a corpse-eater by night.
behavior: Takes blood or organs, often from the pregnant or the sick, and digs up fresh graves. Spanish writers recorded it from the 1500s.
license_note: Folklore recorded in the 16th century; own description.
sensitivity_note: unverified, wiki only (two Wikipedia pages read, no non-wiki source read). Capiz is tied to the term; people with X-linked dystonia parkinsonism on Panay have been branded aswang and shunned. Never imply a real region or illness; keep it generic and monstrous.

name: Manananggal
looks: A woman whose upper body splits off, sprouts bat wings and flies, leaving the legs behind.
behavior: Hunts at night for sleeping pregnant women with a long tongue. Salt, garlic or ash on the left-behind legs kills it at dawn.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Believed in parts of Capiz, Iloilo, Bohol and Antique, with encounters still told. Do not tie it to those places.
reads_at_16x20: yes: winged torso with dangling guts

name: Tikbalang
looks: A tall, bony humanoid with a horse's head and hooves and limbs so long the knees rise above its head when it squats.
behavior: Leads travelers around in circles in forest and mountain. A shirt worn inside out or a spoken request to pass breaks the spell.
license_note: Folklore; the horse form is later than Spanish contact; own description.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Some people still hold that a tikbalang guards a balete tree, and balete trees were sacred. Keep it a hostile monster.
reads_at_16x20: yes: horse head on tall thin body

name: Kapre
looks: A tall, dark, hairy tree giant in a loincloth that sits in big trees.
behavior: Pranks travelers and avenges a cut-down tree; may befriend a person for life.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. The page says the name and image grew from colonial prejudice against dark-skinned Aeta/Negrito people, so a design risks reading as a stereotype of a real ethnic group. Recommend skipping or a heavy redesign; owner decides.

name: Sigbin
looks: A hornless goat-like animal with huge ears, a whip tail and a bad smell.
behavior: Walks backward with its head down, can turn invisible, and is said to hunt children's hearts in Holy Week.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Known today in rural Visayas and Mindanao; families said to keep sigbin may be stigmatized. Keep it a wild monster.

name: Tiyanak
looks: A baby or toddler that shows a wizened old face once picked up.
behavior: Cries like an infant in the forest to lure travelers, then attacks.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Tied to unbaptized babies and, in modern belief, aborted fetuses; people use charms today. Avoid a literal baby-killing theme.

name: Wakwak
looks: A bird-like creature with razor wings and long talons.
behavior: Snatches people at night and tears them with its talons; its wingbeats fade as it closes in.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. The page says belief is fading and the tale is now mostly told to children.

name: Berberoka
origin: Philippine folklore, northern Luzon (Apayao, Abra, Ilocos Norte)
looks: A swamp creature; the page gives no body description, so the design would be mine.
behavior: Drains a pond so the fish lie stranded, then floods it back over those who come to gather them.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. The page says nothing about living belief.

name: Amomongo
looks: A man-sized white or hairy ape with long nails that lives in caves.
behavior: Attacks livestock and eats their insides; locals treat it as an animal, not a spirit.
license_note: Cryptid; a folktale 'Amomongo and Iput-Iput' exists but the main reports are from 2008, so folklore age unverified.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. 2008 reports were treated as local news; no sacred status found.

name: Bungisngis
looks: A one-eyed giant with two tusks that is always laughing.
behavior: Strong enough to hurl a buffalo but easily tricked and quick to panic.
license_note: Folklore; the page is a stub, so source depth is thin.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. No sacred or ritual role noted.

name: Bakunawa
looks: A horned sea serpent with a looped tail.
behavior: Rises to swallow the moon, causing eclipses.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. It figured in babaylan rituals and merged with naga and Rahu; some retellings call it a goddess turned serpent. Communities still make noise at eclipses.

name: Pontianak
origin: Malay and Indonesian folklore; Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore
looks: Pale woman with long black hair in a bloodstained white dress that turns monstrous when she strikes.
behavior: A plumeria scent then rot warns of her; in Malay tales she removes organs, and a nail in the neck subdues her. The city of Pontianak takes its name from the legend.
sensitivity_note: unverified, wiki only (two Wikipedia pages read, no non-wiki source read). Widely known and respected in Malaysia and Indonesia; keep it generic and not tied to the real city.
reads_at_16x20: no: reads as a woman in a white dress; add owl or claws

name: Langsuyar
looks: A long-haired woman in a green robe with long nails, or a floating head trailing a spine and entrails.
behavior: Preys on newborns, usually boys, with an owl on the roof. Cutting her nails and hair into the hole in her neck tames her, per Skeat (1900).
license_note: Recorded by Skeat 1900 (public domain; cited through the Wikipedia article, not read directly).
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. In 2013 Kelantan villagers reported one and authorities urged prayer; it is a living fear.

name: Penanggalan
looks: A woman's head with entrails dripping from the neck, glowing like a flame.
behavior: Seeks blood from childbirth and preys on mothers and infants; soaks her organs in vinegar to shrink them. First seen in the 1845 Hikayat Abdullah.
sensitivity_note: unverified, wiki only (two Wikipedia pages read, no non-wiki source read). Birth rites and a healer (bomoh) still answer to it. Overlaps Krasue and Leyak; use only one if the owner wants variety.
reads_at_16x20: yes: flaming head with a tail

name: Toyol
looks: A small near-naked toddler with red eyes and teeth, sometimes green-skinned.
behavior: Raised by a shaman and sent to steal money for its owner.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Scams and sightings were reported in 2009, 2016 and 2019; it is a live belief.

name: Polong and Pelesit
looks: A fingertip-sized woman-spirit (polong) with a grasshopper-like pet (pelesit).
behavior: Sent into a victim's mouth to possess them until a shaman questions it.
license_note: Folklore; Skeat 1900 not read on this point; own description.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Possession and exorcism are living practices, and an accused owner can be harmed.

name: Hantu Raya
looks: A hairy black humanoid with rough grey skin, long teeth and red eyes.
behavior: A familiar a sorcerer keeps for strength; it takes its owner's shape and must get its offering on time.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. A feared familiar spirit; the page gives no belief detail.

name: Pocong
origin: Javanese and Malay folklore; Indonesia and Malaysia
looks: A corpse tied in its burial shroud, hopping because its feet are bound.
behavior: Rises when the shroud ties were not loosed at the grave; unpredictable and sometimes gathers in groups.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Tied to Islamic burial practice, so keep it a generic wrapped undead and avoid a religious frame.

name: Wewe Gombel
looks: A long-breasted woman who nests in a palm crown.
behavior: Takes neglected children and returns them when parents repent; she is hostile in the tale, with a gentle side.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Still told to children as a warning; the page says little more.
reads_at_16x20: yes: tall woman with a palm nest

name: Leyak
looks: A head with heart, lungs and liver hanging below, long tongue and fangs; human by day.
behavior: Haunts graveyards, eats corpses, drinks the blood of pregnant women and newborns, and may take an animal shape.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Balinese still blame illness on leyak and use healers; it is bound up with Hindu-Balinese ritual. Same silhouette as Krasue and Penanggalan.

name: Rangda
looks: A widow-witch with a monstrous mask, long tongue and fangs.
behavior: Rules the leyak and is paraded in temple festivals.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Her mask is kept in a village death temple and used in sacred dance; a ritual figure, not an enemy.

name: Orang Minyak
origin: Malay urban legend; Malaysia and Singapore
looks: A man coated in black grease so he slips free of hands.
behavior: Climbs into houses at night and attacks women.
license_note: Modern origin: first record is a 1957 Singapore newspaper report and a 1958 film, so a modern invention.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Most versions make him a sexual predator; not suitable.

name: Rakshasa
origin: Hindu and Buddhist epics; India and Sri Lanka
looks: A huge shape-changer with fangs, claws and fiery eyes.
behavior: Disrupts sacrifices, eats people and uses illusion to change form.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Villains of the Ramayana, which many Hindus hold sacred; some Buddhist sutras show rakshasa guardians. Ravana is revered by some communities and must not be used as an enemy.

name: Vetala
looks: A thin, ribbed, cold-skinned corpse-spirit with unblinking eyes that hangs upside down in a burning-ground tree.
behavior: Possesses corpses, haunts cremation grounds and poses riddles; Burton's text has it bargain with King Vikram.
license_note: Folklore; the Vetala Panchavimshati is 11th century at the latest; own description.
sensitivity_note: Two sources read (Wikipedia and Burton's Gutenberg text; Burton's page covers the baital's look). The Betal cult is active in Goa and Konkan, where Betal is a temple deity; keep the corpse-spirit, not the deity.

name: Pishacha
looks: A gaunt shape-changer with bulging veins and red eyes.
behavior: Haunts cremation grounds, possesses people and feeds on life energy.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Offerings at some festivals keep it away; it also appears in Thai temple art.

name: Brahmarakshasa
looks: A huge horned figure with a priest's topknot, seen hanging upside down in trees.
behavior: Feeds on flesh and blood; a corrupt priest returns as one, and some stories say it grants boons.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Real shrines in Maharashtra, Kerala and Karnataka receive lamps and offerings; some are venerated as demigods. Avoid a priest-as-demon theme.

behavior: Lures men into the wild and drains their life; the ghost of a woman who died cruelly or in childbirth.
sensitivity_note: unverified, wiki only (two Wikipedia pages read, no non-wiki source read). 'Chudail' is also used for accused women; avoid witch-hunt framing.

behavior: Each brings an illness until an exorcism ritual humbles it before the Buddha's authority.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. A living Sinhalese healing ritual still performed on the south coast; using the masks would borrow a sacred performance. Owner decides.

name: Naga
origin: Hindu, Buddhist, Thai, Khmer and Javanese tradition
looks: Cobra-hooded serpents or half-human beings, often many-headed.
behavior: Guard treasure and water; mostly benevolent but venomous; a Khmer legend has a hostile nine-headed one.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Revered: Thailand made the naga a national symbol in 2022, and many Khmer see themselves as naga descendants. Never an enemy.

name: Garuda
origin: Hindu and Buddhist tradition; India, Thailand, Indonesia
looks: A giant eagle or winged bird-man with a green body and golden wings.
behavior: Vishnu's mount and the sworn enemy of serpents.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. A sacred mount and the national emblem of Thailand and Indonesia. Not usable as an enemy.

name: Makara
looks: A hybrid sea beast with a stag or elephant front and a fish or snake rear.
behavior: Guards gateways and thresholds in temple carvings; mount of Ganga and Varuna.
sensitivity_note: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. A sacred vehicle and temple guardian; most stone taps in Nepal are still carved as makara.
